ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study received ethical approval from the University of Leicester Ethics Committee (ref: 39830).
To reduce experimenter bias, data were analysed after all the participants were recruited and a stopping rule was established prior to data collection.
To achieve this, we recruited 60 younger adults (30 assigned to unspaced and 30 assigned to spaced conditions) and 30 older adults (who completed both spaced and unspaced conditions).
A final sample of 90 participants took part in the study.
The young adult participants were first-and second-year undergraduate students from the School of Psychology and Vision Sciences at the University of Leicester.
Older adult participants were recruited from the local community in Leicester.

Importantly, all participants were classed as native British English speakers: all participants completed their education within the British education system and reported using British English as their primary language from the age of three years.
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.
These assessments verified that all participants had been properly corrected for the specific viewing distance of the experimental screen.
We therefore collected new normative data online, using Prolific, to ensure that the stimuli were appropriate for a UK population.
On each trial, participants were presented with a partial sentence and asked to provide the expected compound word.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: those who completed the unspaced session first and those who completed the spaced session first.
Participants were tested individually in a dimmed room.
Participants were instructed to read each sentence naturally and for comprehension.
Participants were instructed to read each sentence naturally and silently, and to then look toward a fixation point located to the right of the sentence.
Participants were offered breaks approximately every 15 minutes and could take additional breaks as needed.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Recent simulation-based power analyses in reading and eye-tracking (e.g., Schmidtke et al., 2021) emphasize detecting weak main effect slopes (e.g., b = 0.008, as observed in Juhasz, 2018). Consequently, we focused our design and power calculations specifically on detecting critical two-way interactions (e.g., Ageing × AoA, and Spacing × AoA), while adopting a conservative approach to parameter estimation. To reduce experimenter bias, data were analysed after all the participants were recruited and a stopping rule was established prior to data collection. In contrast to compound word studies and AoA using other tasks, eye-tracking evidence concerning the AoA effect remains limited except for Juhasz (2018). We conducted a power analysis, following Elsherif et al. (2019), using Westfall et al.'s (2014) formula for effect size calculation.
table.effect_size_metric_other: Westfall et al.'s (2014) formula for effect size calculation

table.text: Following Elsherif et al. (2019), the power analysis was specified with an effect size of d = 0.063, a residual variance of 0.61, a participant intercept variance of 0.23, an item intercept variance of 0.16, and participant-by-item, participant-slope, and item-slope variances set to 0. PANGEA power calculations indicated that a sample size of 30 participants per experiment (i.e., spaced x unspaced in young adults (Experiments 1 and 2) and spaced x unspaced in older adults (Experiments 3 and 4) reading 209 items would yield statistical power exceeding 1 -ẞ = .80 for the target two-way interaction effects.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Investigating the Relationship Between Age of Acquisition and Compound Words: Age-Related Differences in Processing Spaced and Unspaced Compound Words
table.measured_variables: Measured variables used in Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria: first fixation duration (i.e., duration of initial fixation on a word), ms, single fixation duration (i.e., a word receives one fixation that allows identification prior to the upcoming word being processed during the first pass of a sentence), ms, gaze duration (the sum of fixations on the word prior to the upcoming word in the sentence) , ms and total fixation duration (the total duration of processing of words, including rereading the word), ms.
table.transformations: Continuous variables such as reading times (e.g. gaze durations) may not be normally distributed. Therefore, we will apply log or inverse transformation to these variables to ensure normality. If the pattern of results for transformed and untransformed data is the same, we will present the results for untransformed data for transparency. The remaining data will be placed in the supplementary materials.
table.inference_criteria:
Both Bayesian and frequentist statistical methods will be employed to analyze the data. The Bayesian approach will provide estimates of the effect size, along with 95% credible intervals and probabilities for each effect. The frequentist approach will use the standard p < .05 criteria, with a Holm-Bonferroni correction across all the variables to control the family-wise error rate (FWER).


For the Bayesian models, the minimal sample size of 30 young and 30 older adults may still return a Bayes factor that is uninformative and represents evidence in favor of neither model (i.e. 1/3–3). This is not problematic, as Bayesian methods allow for incremental data collection. If the Bayes factor remains uninformative with 60 participants, we can simply increase the sample size until the model provides conclusive evidence in either direction.

Frequentist Analyses

For the frequentist models, a Holm-Bonferroni correction will be applied across all the key variables to control the FWER. This is preferred over the Bonferroni correction, which is recommended for eye-tracking methods (Von der Malsburg & Angele, 2017). The Holm-Bonferroni correction offers a more powerful test than the Bonferroni correction, allowing for not only a reduction in Type I error but also Type II error.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria: All trials were removed from the analysis for track losses on the pretarget, compound word, or post-target word or if the initial fixation on the sentence was not on the first region (Juhasz & Sheridan, 2020). Eye movement data will be excluded due to tracker loss or technical difficulties. Fixations shorter than 80ms and longer than 1200ms will be removed. For each reading time measure, data more than 2.5 SDs from the mean for each participant for each condition will be excluded.
table.missing_data_handling: Data partially missing because participant quit study halfway through will be excluded; if applicable, data partially missing due to unforeseen software errors will be included in the main categorical analyses. However, any missing data will follow the recommendations by Woods et al. (2023).
table.exploratory_analyses: To ensure that any divergence from the findings of Juhasz (2018) is not the result of Bayesian, as opposed to frequentist, statistics being used, we will also conduct the analyses using general linear mixed modeling (GLMM) only for young adults. This will allow us to calculate measures of effect size using the MuMIn package.

table.manipulated_variables:
Manipulated variables

To examine the effects of spacing, age, and AoA on compound word processing, we will employ a regression analysis. The outcome variables will be the fixation duration measures (first fixation, single fixation, gaze duration, and total fixation duration) for the target word. The predictors will include:

Letter Length of the compound word: The number of letters in the compound word.

Frequency: The frequency of the compound word, ranging from 1 to 7, with higher values indicating higher frequency.

Familiarity: A measure of how familiar the compound word is to British speakers, ranging from 1 to 7, with higher values indicating higher familiarity.

Imageability: A measure of how easily British speakers can evoke a mental image associated with the compound word, ranging from 1 to 7, with higher values indicating higher imageability.

Log AoA: The age at which the compound word was acquired, expressed in log transformation, with higher values indicating earlier acquisition.

Semantic Transparency: A measure of how transparent the meaning of the compound word is, ranging from 1 to 7, with higher values indicating higher transparency.

Lexeme Meaning Dominance: A measure of the relative importance of the first and second lexemes in determining the meaning of the entire compound word, ranging from 1 to 7, with higher values indicating greater dominance of the first lexeme and lower values indicating greater dominance of the second lexeme.

Morpheme Length (First and Second): The number of letters in the first and second morphemes of the compound word.

Morpheme Frequency (First and Second): The frequency of the first and second morphemes of the compound word, ranging from 1 to 7, with higher values indicating higher frequency.

Morpheme Familiarity (First and Second): A measure of how familiar the first and second morphemes are to British speakers, ranging from 1 to 7, with higher values indicating higher familiarity.

Log AoA of Morphemes (First and Second): The age at which the first and second morphemes of the compound word were acquired, expressed in log transformation, with higher values indicating earlier acquisition.

Morpheme Imageability (First and Second): A measure of how easily British speakers can evoke a mental image associated with the first and second morphemes of the compound word, ranging from 1 to 7, with higher values indicating higher imageability.

Place of articulation (Bilabial, Labiodental, Dental, Labiovelar, Postalveolar, Alveolar, Palatal, Palatal-alveolar, Glottal, Velar): A set of dummy variables indicating the presence or absence of specific vowel sounds in the compound word.

Voiced: A dummy variable indicating whether the compound word begins in a voiced consonant.

Ageing: A binary variable indicating whether the participant is a younger or older adult.

Spacing: A binary variable indicating whether the compound word is presented in unspaced or spaced format.

The data for the regression analysis will be obtained from a norming study conducted for the current project. Frequency information will be obtained from the SUBTLEX-UK database (van Heuven et al., 2014).

This comprehensive regression analysis will allow us to examine the interactive effects of spacing, age, and AoA on fixation duration measures, providing insights into the underlying mechanisms of compound word processing in the context of age-related changes and lexical factors.
table.statistical_tests:
To determine which hypothesis our data supports, we will construct Bayesian mixed models using the brms package in R (Burkner, 2019). These models will provide estimates of the effect size, along with 95% credible intervals and probabilities for each effect. We will construct separate models for each fixation duration measure (first fixation duration, gaze duration, total reading time, and regression probability).
For the reading time measures, we will use inverse reading time as the outcome variable. This approach has been shown to be more accurate than log transformation or untransformed reaction time (Brysbaert & Stevens, 2018). 
We will start with a baseline model that includes the following variables:
Phonetic complexity variables: These include bilabial, labiodental, dental, labiovelar, postalveolar, alveolar, palatal, palatal-alveolar, glottal, and velar.
Word frequency: This is the frequency of the compound word in SUBTLEX-UK (van Heuven et al., 2014).
Word length: This is the number of characters in the compound word.
Morpheme frequency: This is the frequency of each morpheme in the compound word, also obtained from SUBTLEX-UK.
Next, we will add individual fixed effects for each of the following variables to the model:
Familiarity: This is a measure of how familiar the compound word is to British speakers.
Imageability: This is a measure of how easily British speakers can evoke a mental image associated with the compound word.
Log AoA: This is the age at which the compound word was acquired, expressed in log transformation.
Semantic transparency: This is a measure of how transparent the meaning of the compound word is.
Lexeme meaning dominance: This is a measure of the relative importance of the first and second lexemes in determining the meaning of the entire compound word.
Morpheme familiarity (first and second): These are measures of how familiar the first and second morphemes of the compound word are to British speakers.
Log AoA of morphemes (first and second): These are measures of the age at which the first and second morphemes of the compound word were acquired, expressed in log transformation.
Morpheme imageability (first and second): These are measures of how easily British speakers can evoke a mental image associated with the first and second morphemes of the compound word.
Voiced: This is a dummy variable indicating whether the compound word begins in a voiced consonant.
By-participant and by-item random intercepts and slopes will be included for each fixed effect in the models. This will allow us to account for individual differences and item-specific effects.
Priors for all models will be weakly informative. We will use Normal priors with mean 0 and standard deviation 10 for the model intercept and for each fixed effect and standard deviation parameter. A regularisation of 2 will be used on the covariance matrix of random effects.
Each model will be run with four chains of 5000 iterations each, with 1000 iterations being treated as warmup. If any model returns parameters with an Rhat above 1, further iterations will be added.
In summary, our Bayesian mixed models analysis will provide a comprehensive assessment of the effects of spacing, age, AoA, and other lexical factors on compound word processing. This analysis will allow us to draw robust conclusions about the underlying mechanisms of compound word processing in the context of age-related changes and lexical factors.
table.research_questions:
We will utilize four fixation duration measures to assess AoA effects in compound words: first-fixation duration, single fixation duration, gaze duration, and total fixation duration. These measures reflect different stages of lexical processing and provide insights into the underlying mechanisms responsible for AoA effects.
First-Fixation Duration
First-fixation duration represents the time spent fixating on a word during the initial pass through the sentence. It is a sensitive index of early lexical processing and is particularly relevant to the mapping theory (Ellis & Lambon-Ralph, 2000; Dirix & Duyck, 2017a).

Single Fixation Duration
Single fixation duration measures the duration of the initial fixation when a word receives one fixation during a reader's first pass through the sentence. This suggests that the reader has fully identified the word prior to moving their eyes to the next word.
Gaze Duration
Gaze duration reflects the total time spent fixating on a word before the reader moves their eyes to the next word. This summed measure indicates full lexical access and is relevant to both the mapping and representation theories.
Total Fixation Duration
Total fixation duration includes rereading the word and is considered a late measure of processing that also incorporates integrative processes. It is relevant to the representation theory (Brysbaert et al., 2000), which posits that AoA effects are more pronounced during later stages of processing.

Simple Effects

We hypothesize the following simple effects:

Younger adults will exhibit shorter fixation durations compared to older adults for all measures (Rayner et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2023).

Early-acquired words will exhibit shorter fixation durations compared to late-acquired words for all measures (e.g. Juhasz & Rayner, 2003, 2006; Juhasz, 2018; Juhasz & Sheridan, 2020).

Spaced compound words will exhibit shorter fixation durations compared to unspaced compound words for all measures (e.g. Frisson et al., 2007).

In addition to our replication of Juhasz (2018), we will follow the hypotheses based on the two new theories, as the previous study did not have hypotheses. Following the representation theory (Brysbaert et al., 2000) is correct, we predict that the more semantics is involved in word recognition, the larger the AoA effect. The AoA effect should be observed in unspaced and spaced compound word reading task, the magnitude of effect sizes should be larger in spaced compound word than unspaced compound word, irrespective of ageing.
In addition to replicating the findings of Juhasz (2018), we will investigate the following hypotheses based on the two new theories:

Representation Theory (Brysbaert et al., 2000): The more semantics is involved in word recognition, the larger the AoA effect.

Mapping Theory (Ellis & Lambon Ralph, 2000): AoA effects will be observed across both younger and older adults, together with spaced and unspaced compound words but the effect size will be larger in older adults and for spaced compound words. This is because spaced compound words are more distinctive and require greater processing effort, particularly for older adults with reduced neural plasticity. In addition, spaced compound words are more perceptually distinctive than unspaced compound words.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
We will employ a mixed design to examine AoA effects in compound words, encompassing both within-item and between-subject manipulations.
All participants will complete all items within each eye-tracking experiment. This ensures that each participant encounters both unspaced and spaced compound words, allowing for a direct comparison of processing patterns. To minimize potential order effects, the order of presentation of unspaced and spaced compound word experiments will be randomized across participants. This within-item design will enable us to capture the effects of AoA and spacing within individual participants, providing insights into the underlying processing mechanisms.
Two age groups will be compared: younger adults and older adults. Each age group will consist of 30 participants. This between-subject manipulation will allow us to examine age-related differences in AoA effects, particularly in the context of spaced compound words. By comparing the processing patterns of younger and older adults, we can gain a deeper understanding of how age-related changes influence the processing of compound words.
table.randomization: Item order is fully randomised during the experiment.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
Young adults: Participants will be recruited from the University of Leicester community; they must be 18 years of age or older, native UK English speakers with no known history of dyslexia. 
Older adults: Participants will be recruited from Leicestershire community; they must be 55 years of age or older, native UK English speakers with no known history of dyslexia.
table.sample_size_rationale:
We aim to collect a minimum of 1600 data points per cell of the experiment design. This corresponds to 12540 observations (60 participants * 209 items), which will provide sufficient power to assess the interaction between spacing, age, and the 15 psycholinguistic factors. To achieve this sample size, we will recruit 30 young adults who will participate in two eye-tracking experiments. However, there are several challenges in terms of recruiting older adults, thus 30 older adults will complete both the spaced and unspaced eye-tracking experiment. In each experiment, participants will be presented with 209 unspaced and 209 spaced compound words. This will ensure that each participant provides a comprehensive dataset for both unspaced and spaced compound words, allowing for a thorough examination of the effects of spacing and age on compound word processing.
The proposed sample size, which is based on power calculations, is expected to yield a Bayes factor (BF) of 1/3-3, indicating that the data provide insufficient evidence to favor either model. However, this is not a concern, as Bayesian methods allow us to iteratively increase the sample size until our model provides conclusive evidence in favour of either hypothesis or model. This iterative approach ensures that our findings are robust and supported by sufficient data.
table.stopping_rule:
Data collection will stop once data for 30 young adults for each experiment and 30 older adults in total has been collected. Replacements will be recruited based on the exclusion criterion outlined later as needed.  Analysis of the data will not begin until the complete sample of 30 young and 30 older adults has been collected. 
Following data collection, we will calculate a Bayes Factor to assess whether there is evidence for or against the critical interaction between spacing, age and AoA. The aim is to replicate the effect of compound word AoA on first fixation, single fixation, gaze duration, and total fixation duration on the target word. While Juhasz (2018) demonstrated the effect of AoA on these measures, the study did not explore the interaction between AoA, ageing, and spacing. The generated Bayes factors will be used to determine whether a significant effect exists in each measure.
If the Bayes factors for the measures remain uninformative with 30 young and 30 older adults, we will continue testing participants and incorporating their data into our analysis until the Bayes factor indicates evidence in favour of either the null or alternative hypothesis. This iterative approach will ensure that we have sufficient data to draw a robust conclusion about the interaction between spacing, age, and AoA in compound word processing.

First-fixation duration represents the time spent fixating on a word during the initial pass through the sentence. It is a sensitive index of early lexical processing and is particularly relevant to the mapping theory (Ellis & Lambon-Ralph, 2000; Dirix & Duyck, 2017a).

Single Fixation Duration
Single fixation duration measures the duration of the initial fixation when a word receives one fixation during a reader's first pass through the sentence. This suggests that the reader has fully identified the word prior to moving their eyes to the next word.
Gaze Duration
Gaze duration reflects the total time spent fixating on a word before the reader moves their eyes to the next word. This summed measure indicates full lexical access and is relevant to both the mapping and representation theories.
Total Fixation Duration
Total fixation duration includes rereading the word and is considered a late measure of processing that also incorporates integrative processes. It is relevant to the representation theory (Brysbaert et al., 2000), which posits that AoA effects are more pronounced during later stages of processing.

Simple Effects

We hypothesize the following simple effects:

Younger adults will exhibit shorter fixation durations compared to older adults for all measures (Rayner et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2023).

Early-acquired words will exhibit shorter fixation durations compared to late-acquired words for all measures (e.g. Juhasz & Rayner, 2003, 2006; Juhasz, 2018; Juhasz & Sheridan, 2020).

Spaced compound words will exhibit shorter fixation durations compared to unspaced compound words for all measures (e.g. Frisson et al., 2007).

In addition to our replication of Juhasz (2018), we will follow the hypotheses based on the two new theories, as the previous study did not have hypotheses. Following the representation theory (Brysbaert et al., 2000) is correct, we predict that the more semantics is involved in word recognition, the larger the AoA effect. The AoA effect should be observed in unspaced and spaced compound word reading task, the magnitude of effect sizes should be larger in spaced compound word than unspaced compound word, irrespective of ageing.
In addition to replicating the findings of Juhasz (2018), we will investigate the following hypotheses based on the two new theories:

Representation Theory (Brysbaert et al., 2000): The more semantics is involved in word recognition, the larger the AoA effect.

Mapping Theory (Ellis & Lambon Ralph, 2000): AoA effects will be observed across both younger and older adults, together with spaced and unspaced compound words but the effect size will be larger in older adults and for spaced compound words. This is because spaced compound words are more distinctive and require greater processing effort, particularly for older adults with reduced neural plasticity. In addition, spaced compound words are more perceptually distinctive than unspaced compound words.", "Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.", "No blinding is involved in this study.", "We will employ a mixed design to examine AoA effects in compound words, encompassing both within-item and between-subject manipulations.
All participants will complete all items within each eye-tracking experiment. This ensures that each participant encounters both unspaced and spaced compound words, allowing for a direct comparison of processing patterns. To minimize potential order effects, the order of presentation of unspaced and spaced compound word experiments will be randomized across participants. This within-item design will enable us to capture the effects of AoA and spacing within individual participants, providing insights into the underlying processing mechanisms.
Two age groups will be compared: younger adults and older adults. Each age group will consist of 30 participants. This between-subject manipulation will allow us to examine age-related differences in AoA effects, particularly in the context of spaced compound words. By comparing the processing patterns of younger and older adults, we can gain a deeper understanding of how age-related changes influence the processing of compound words.", "Item order is fully randomised during the experiment.", "Registration prior to creation of data", "Young adults: Participants will be recruited from the University of Leicester community; they must be 18 years of age or older, native UK English speakers with no known history of dyslexia.
Older adults: Participants will be recruited from Leicestershire community; they must be 55 years of age or older, native UK English speakers with no known history of dyslexia.", "30 young and 30 older adults.", "We aim to collect a minimum of 1600 data points per cell of the experiment design. This corresponds to 12540 observations (60 participants * 209 items), which will provide sufficient power to assess the interaction between spacing, age, and the 15 psycholinguistic factors. To achieve this sample size, we will recruit 30 young adults who will participate in two eye-tracking experiments. However, there are several challenges in terms of recruiting older adults, thus 30 older adults will complete both the spaced and unspaced eye-tracking experiment. In each experiment, participants will be presented with 209 unspaced and 209 spaced compound words. This will ensure that each participant provides a comprehensive dataset for both unspaced and spaced compound words, allowing for a thorough examination of the effects of spacing and age on compound word processing.
The proposed sample size, which is based on power calculations, is expected to yield a Bayes factor (BF) of 1/3-3, indicating that the data provide insufficient evidence to favor either model. However, this is not a concern, as Bayesian methods allow us to iteratively increase the sample size until our model provides conclusive evidence in favour of either hypothesis or model. This iterative approach ensures that our findings are robust and supported by sufficient data.", "Data collection will stop once data for 30 young adults for each experiment and 30 older adults in total has been collected. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. summary_table.ethics_statements: The study received ethical approval from the University of Leicester Ethics Committee (ref: 39830).
live_data_statements: To reduce experimenter bias, data were analysed after all the participants were recruited and a stopping rule was established prior to data collection.
To achieve this, we recruited 60 younger adults (30 assigned to unspaced and 30 assigned to spaced conditions) and 30 older adults (who completed both spaced and unspaced conditions).
A final sample of 90 participants took part in the study.
The young adult participants were first-and second-year undergraduate students from the School of Psychology and Vision Sciences at the University of Leicester.
Older adult participants were recruited from the local community in Leicester.

Importantly, all participants were classed as native British English speakers: all participants completed their education within the British education system and reported using British English as their primary language from the age of three years.
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.
These assessments verified that all participants had been properly corrected for the specific viewing distance of the experimental screen.
We therefore collected new normative data online, using Prolific, to ensure that the stimuli were appropriate for a UK population.
On each trial, participants were presented with a partial sentence and asked to provide the expected compound word.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: those who completed the unspaced session first and those who completed the spaced session first.
Participants were tested individually in a dimmed room.
Participants were instructed to read each sentence naturally and for comprehension.
Participants were instructed to read each sentence naturally and silently, and to then look toward a fixation point located to the right of the sentence.
Participants were offered breaks approximately every 15 minutes and could take additional breaks as needed.

**`setwd()` in the code**

**2 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

text.text: This repository also includes an R Markdown script to reproduce all analyses and generate the manuscript.
What is the AoA effect?
Linguistic experience significantly shapes how language is acquired and processed.
In turn, linguistic experience subsequently influences both cognitive functions and social interactions (Kidd et al., 2018; Perfetti, 2007 Perfetti, , 2017)).
text.formatted: In turn, linguistic experience subsequently influences both cognitive functions and social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Kidd et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Perfetti, 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Perfetti, , 2017))</ref>.

text.text: The age at which a word is learned, its age of acquisition (AoA), is a key element of this linguistic experience and is a robust predictor of the efficiency and speed of word retrieval (Carroll & White, 1973).
text.formatted: The age at which a word is learned, its age of acquisition (AoA), is a key element of this linguistic experience and is a robust predictor of the efficiency and speed of word retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Carroll & White, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: It is a truism that words learned earlier in life (e.g., unicorn) are processed more quickly and with greater accuracy than words acquired later (e.g., taxes).

This AoA effect has been documented across diverse languages, experimental designs and modalities of language processing, in standard behavioural measures, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging (see review by Elsherif et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This AoA effect has been documented across diverse languages, experimental designs and modalities of language processing, in standard behavioural measures, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging (see review by <ref type="bibr">Elsherif et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Although critics have suggested that the AoA effect can be reduced to other lexical-semantic properties, such as word frequency and concreteness (Smolik & Filip, 2022; Strain et al., 1995; Zevin & Seidenberg, 2002 , 2004), an independent influence of AoA has been reported in several language processing tasks, such as word naming, lexical decision, memory tasks and picture naming (e.g. Catling et al., 2021; Catling & Elsherif, 2020; Davies et al., 2017;  see review by Elsherif et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Although critics have suggested that the AoA effect can be reduced to other lexical-semantic properties, such as word frequency and concreteness <ref type="bibr">(Smolik & Filip, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Strain et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Zevin & Seidenberg, 2002</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2004)</ref>, an independent influence of AoA has been reported in several language processing tasks, such as word naming, lexical decision, memory tasks and picture naming (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Catling et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Catling & Elsherif, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Davies et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> see review by <ref type="bibr">Elsherif et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, it is difficult to attribute the AoA effect to mere effects of frequency or concreteness (Brysbaert, 2017; Juhasz et al., 2025).
text.formatted: As a result, it is difficult to attribute the AoA effect to mere effects of frequency or concreteness <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brysbaert, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Juhasz et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, the bulk of research on the AoA effect has been restricted to young adults, largely using traditional, response-based tasks (e.g., lexical decision, word naming, memory), and with a focus on monomorphemic words (e.g., cat) (see review by Elsherif et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Crucially, the bulk of research on the AoA effect has been restricted to young adults, largely using traditional, response-based tasks (e.g., lexical decision, word naming, memory), and with a focus on monomorphemic words (e.g., cat) (see review by <ref type="bibr">Elsherif et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, there is limited understanding of how AoA effects manifest in older adults and during the processing of complex words, such as compound words (e.g., sunshine), particularly within naturalistic language processing contexts such as text reading.

Given that both ageing and item complexity can shape how words are accessed and represented in the brain, we were particularly interested in how the AoA effect influences word processing in older adults, especially during the processing of spaced and unspaced compound words.
The present study moves beyond investigations of the AoA effect limited to monomorphemic words to compound words.
Specifically, we examined how differences in age (young vs. older adulthood) and the visual presentation of these words (spaced vs. unspaced) influence AoA effects.
We also measured eye movements during sentence reading, which is a more ecologically valid task of reading than the isolated word recognition tasks typically used in this field.
Below, we provide the theoretical background to the AoA effect, review the compound word literature, and present the current study.
There are two explanations for the AoA effect.

First, the Representation Account posits that the AoA effect directly shapes the meaning of the word's representation (i.e., semantic), influencing the richness and depth of its connections within the mental lexicon (Brysbaert et al., 2000; Brysbaert & Ghyselinck, 2006; Steyvers & Tenenbaum, 2005; van Loon-Vervoorn, 1989).
text.formatted: First, the Representation Account posits that the AoA effect directly shapes the meaning of the word's representation (i.e., semantic), influencing the richness and depth of its connections within the mental lexicon <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brysbaert et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Brysbaert & Ghyselinck, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Steyvers & Tenenbaum, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">van Loon-Vervoorn, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: According to the Representation Account, words learned earlier are situated more centrally, or in the "hub", of the semantic network, resulting in stronger and more elaborate semantic connections to other conceptual nodes.

The second account, Mapping Theory (Ellis & Lambon Ralph, 2000; Monaghan & Ellis, 2010), posits that the AoA effect influences the robustness of a word's various representations, including its orthographic (spelling), phonological (sound), and semantic (meaning) forms.
text.formatted: The second account, Mapping Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ellis & Lambon Ralph, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Monaghan & Ellis, 2010)</ref>, posits that the AoA effect influences the robustness of a word's various representations, including its orthographic (spelling), phonological (sound), and semantic (meaning) forms.

text.text: According to Mapping Theory, words acquired early in life benefit from a period of heightened neuroplasticity during early development.
This neuroplasticity allows for words to be more easily consolidated, and for the formation of stronger and more interconnected mappings between the word's different representational systems.
This greater integration facilitates more rapid and efficient retrieval.

Conversely, words learned later in life must either leverage the established connections of early-acquired words or incur a processing cost, because modifying the existing, rigid neural network is challenging.
While the Representation Account and Mapping Theory propose different cognitive mechanisms for the AoA effect, these are not mutually exclusive.

The proposed Integrated Account therefore attempts to fully explain the AoA effect by combining elements of both the Representation Account and Mapping Theory (Catling & Elsherif, 2020; Chang et al., 2019; Cortese et al., 2020; Elsherif & Catling, 2023; Menenti & Burani, 2007; Wang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The proposed Integrated Account therefore attempts to fully explain the AoA effect by combining elements of both the Representation Account and Mapping Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Catling & Elsherif, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Chang et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Cortese et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Elsherif & Catling, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Menenti & Burani, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Wang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: According to the Integrated Account, the AoA effect arises due to developmental learning experiences progressively shaping lexical processing.
Early-acquired words occupy a central position within the semantic hub, in line with the Representation Account.
However, they also benefit from the cross-modal mapping emphasised by Mapping Theory.
Because earlyacquired words are consolidated during periods of peak neuroplasticity, the connections between their orthographic, phonological and semantic forms are more deeply entrenched.

The central position of early-acquired words within the semantic lexicon, together with the more entrenched mapping between different levels of lexical representation, fosters a more accessible network for early-acquired words (e.g., Brysbaert & Ellis, 2016; Chang et al., 2019; Elsherif et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The central position of early-acquired words within the semantic lexicon, together with the more entrenched mapping between different levels of lexical representation, fosters a more accessible network for early-acquired words (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Brysbaert & Ellis, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Chang et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Elsherif et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The age at which a word is acquired therefore fundamentally impacts how that word is represented, processed, and retrieved from memory.
Evidence for the AoA effect from eye-tracking
The Integrated Account of the AoA effect has mainly been tested using responsebased measures, which only reflect the end-stage outcome of underlying cognitive processes (Rayner, 1998).
text.formatted: The Integrated Account of the AoA effect has mainly been tested using responsebased measures, which only reflect the end-stage outcome of underlying cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Rayner, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, eye-tracking while reading allows researchers to directly and temporally measure the cognitive processes involved in reading, without requiring an overt behavioral response (Rayner, 1998).
text.formatted: In contrast, eye-tracking while reading allows researchers to directly and temporally measure the cognitive processes involved in reading, without requiring an overt behavioral response <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Rayner, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Eye-movement metrics can be separated into two stages, based on the aspect of word processing they are believed to capture.

Earlier-stage measures consist of first fixation duration (FFD; i.e. the duration of the initial fixation of a given word); single fixation duration (SFD; i.e. the duration of the single fixation of a given word, in cases where the word is fixated only once before the eye moves rightward to the subsequent word, during the first pass of the sentence); and gaze duration (GD; i.e. the sum duration of fixations of a given word, before the eye moves rightward to the subsequent word in the sentence).
These measures are argued to reflect initial word recognition and lexical access.

Later-stage measures, such as total fixation duration (TFD; the total duration of fixations on a given word, including all refixations) are argued to reflect post-lexical processing, such as semantic integration.

Although existing work is limited for the AoA effect in eye-tracking, studies have repeatedly shown that the AoA effect emerges in measures of both first-pass reading and total reading times, with earlier-acquired words receiving shorter fixations (see review by Elsherif et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Although existing work is limited for the AoA effect in eye-tracking, studies have repeatedly shown that the AoA effect emerges in measures of both first-pass reading and total reading times, with earlier-acquired words receiving shorter fixations (see review by <ref type="bibr">Elsherif et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Early studies established that AoA influences first-pass measures and the late measure of TFD, independently of word frequency (Juhasz & Rayner, 2003 , 2006; Juhasz et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Early studies established that AoA influences first-pass measures and the late measure of TFD, independently of word frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Juhasz & Rayner, 2003</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Juhasz et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern has since been replicated in ecologically valid contexts, such as novel reading (Dirix & Duyck, 2017a , 2017b), and across diverse linguistic backgrounds (Guedea et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This pattern has since been replicated in ecologically valid contexts, such as novel reading <ref type="bibr">(Dirix & Duyck, 2017a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">, 2017b)</ref>, and across diverse linguistic backgrounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Guedea et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, survival analyses suggest the AoA effect emerges as early as 158 ms into the initial fixation (Juhasz & Sheridan, 2020), supporting the view that early-acquired words benefit from immediate processing advantages.
text.formatted: Notably, survival analyses suggest the AoA effect emerges as early as 158 ms into the initial fixation <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Juhasz & Sheridan, 2020)</ref>, supporting the view that early-acquired words benefit from immediate processing advantages.

text.text: However, the magnitude of this effect appears to modulate with age: while children exhibit pronounced AoA effects, these diminish in young adulthood (Guedea et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, the magnitude of this effect appears to modulate with age: while children exhibit pronounced AoA effects, these diminish in young adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Guedea et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, despite the theoretical importance of cumulative linguistic experience, no research to date has used eyetracking to investigate how the AoA effect manifests in older adults.
Although studies have yet to investigate the influence of word AoA on older adults' eye movements during reading behaviour, studies have examined its impact on standard behavioural task performance.

For instance, Baumgaertner and Tompkins (1998) reported word AoA effects in 29 older adults (aged 52-74 years) in an auditory lexical decision task, with early-acquired words recognised more quickly than late-acquired words (also see Hodgson & Ellis, 1998, who observed a similar AoA effect in picture naming).
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Baumgaertner and Tompkins (1998)</ref> reported word AoA effects in 29 older adults (aged 52-74 years) in an auditory lexical decision task, with early-acquired words recognised more quickly than late-acquired words (also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Hodgson & Ellis, 1998</ref>, who observed a similar AoA effect in picture naming).

text.text: Additional work by Morrison et al. (2003, Experiment 2) reported word AoA effects in 30 younger adults (aged 18-24 years) and 30 older adults (aged 65-83 years) in reading aloud, with earlyacquired words processed more quickly than late-acquired words.
text.formatted: Additional work by <ref type="bibr">Morrison et al. (2003, Experiment 2)</ref> reported word AoA effects in 30 younger adults (aged 18-24 years) and 30 older adults (aged 65-83 years) in reading aloud, with earlyacquired words processed more quickly than late-acquired words.

text.text: Similarly, Davies et al. (2017) used lexical decision (recognition) and visual word naming (production) tasks to assess the variation in psycholinguistic effects across the lifespan, from childhood into old age (from eight to 83 years) in 535 readers.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Davies et al. (2017)</ref> used lexical decision (recognition) and visual word naming (production) tasks to assess the variation in psycholinguistic effects across the lifespan, from childhood into old age (from eight to 83 years) in 535 readers.

text.text: Davies et al. found that the AoA effect influenced response times and accuracy levels across both tasks, with later-acquired words being more difficult to recognise and produce than early-acquired words.However, the magnitude of the AoA effect is largest in youngest children: its influence steadily decreases with increasing reader age.

For instance, Davies et al. (2017) observed that in older adults, the AoA effect was smaller in lexical decision tasks or disappeared entirely in visual word naming (see also Assink et al., 2003, who observed a similar pattern of findings with a similar design).
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Davies et al. (2017)</ref> observed that in older adults, the AoA effect was smaller in lexical decision tasks or disappeared entirely in visual word naming (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Assink et al., 2003</ref>, who observed a similar pattern of findings with a similar design).

text.text: Furthermore, Trudeau-Meisner et al. (2025) investigated the role of AoA, contextual diversity and semantic diversity in picture-naming ability across ageing and bilingualism, observing that early-acquired words were named more efficiently than lateacquired words where the effect wanes in older adulthood.
text.formatted: Furthermore, <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Trudeau-Meisner et al. (2025)</ref> investigated the role of AoA, contextual diversity and semantic diversity in picture-naming ability across ageing and bilingualism, observing that early-acquired words were named more efficiently than lateacquired words where the effect wanes in older adulthood.

text.text: One explanation for this decline is the cumulative frequency hypothesis:,while early-acquired words are are typically encountered more frequently than later-acquired words, these later-acquired words also begin to be processed more similarly to early-acquired words with increasing reader age, due to cumulative exposure over the lifespan (Davies et al., 2017; Lewis, 1999; but see Ghyselinck et al., 2004).
text.formatted: One explanation for this decline is the cumulative frequency hypothesis:,while early-acquired words are are typically encountered more frequently than later-acquired words, these later-acquired words also begin to be processed more similarly to early-acquired words with increasing reader age, due to cumulative exposure over the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Davies et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Lewis, 1999</ref>; but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Ghyselinck et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Collectively, these behavioural findings indicate that while the AoA effect is robust across the lifespan, its predictive power and magnitude are not constant, generally diminishing in older adults where it can be task-dependent, often disappearing in production tasks like naming.

The majority of work on the AoA effect has been in monomorphemic words and findings may not directly translate to compound words, which represent the majority of Englishlanguage words (Mousikou et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The majority of work on the AoA effect has been in monomorphemic words and findings may not directly translate to compound words, which represent the majority of Englishlanguage words <ref type="bibr">(Mousikou et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The majority of words in the world are complex; compound words are a key example of complex words, and are commonplace in various languages such as English, Chinese and Finnish (Bertram & Hyona, 2003; Elsherif et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The majority of words in the world are complex; compound words are a key example of complex words, and are commonplace in various languages such as English, Chinese and Finnish <ref type="bibr">(Bertram & Hyona, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Elsherif et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Wang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In English, compound words (e.g. "airport") are formed from two lexemes: the modifier (e.g. "air" in "airport") and the head (i.e. "port" in "airport").

The modifier narrows the semantic domain of the head (e.g. air specifies that an airport is a port for aeroplanes rather than boats; Benczes, 2005 Benczes, , 2014 Benczes, , 2015;; Günther et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The modifier narrows the semantic domain of the head (e.g. air specifies that an airport is a port for aeroplanes rather than boats; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Benczes, 2005</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Benczes, , 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Benczes, , 2015;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Günther et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The head sets the broader semantic category, establishes the morphosyntactic features of the compound word as a whole, and establishes the word class 1 .
Compound words are, by definition, polysyllabic.
Thus, as compared to monosyllabic words, compound words have a more complex orthography and phonology and require more processing time (Cortese & Schock, 2013).
text.formatted: Thus, as compared to monosyllabic words, compound words have a more complex orthography and phonology and require more processing time <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Cortese & Schock, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This extended processing time allows the word's semantic properties to play a more significant role in the overall recognition of compound words (Elsherif et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This extended processing time allows the word's semantic properties to play a more significant role in the overall recognition of compound words <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Elsherif et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the processing of compound words is qualitatively different to that of monomorphemic words.
It is therefore not appropriate to generalise findings from monomorphemic words to morphologically complex words such as compound words.
The spacing within English compound words may also influence processing.

English compound words show variation in their orthographic form or spatial layout, and are typically categorised as open/spaced (e.g., "ice cream"), hyphenated (e.g., "long-term"), and closed/unspaced (e.g., "blackboard").
This classification is not always rigid, as different dictionaries may disagree on the proper spacing of certain compounds (Juhasz et al., 2005; Kuperman & Bertram, 2013).
text.formatted: This classification is not always rigid, as different dictionaries may disagree on the proper spacing of certain compounds <ref type="bibr">(Juhasz et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Kuperman & Bertram, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Broader evidence indicates that even minimal changes in the presentation of the compound word's spatial layout can fundamentally shift how the compound word is processed, specifically in terms of its morphemic salience (how easily the component parts are recognised) and the semantic relationship between its constituents (Bertram, 2011; Elsherif et al., 2019; Elsherif & Catling, 2023 , 2024; Frisson et al., 2007; Inhoff et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Broader evidence indicates that even minimal changes in the presentation of the compound word's spatial layout can fundamentally shift how the compound word is processed, specifically in terms of its morphemic salience (how easily the component parts are recognised) and the semantic relationship between its constituents <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bertram, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Elsherif et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Elsherif & Catling, 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Frisson et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Inhoff et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: A spaced presentation consistently encourages morphological decomposition, necessitating an additional processing step: the need to merge the two lexemes to access the meaning of the compound word.

This requirement arises because the spaced format introduces competition between the individual constituent meanings and the meaning of the compound as a whole (Brooks & de Garcia, 2015; Kuperman, 2013).
text.formatted: This requirement arises because the spaced format introduces competition between the individual constituent meanings and the meaning of the compound as a whole <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brooks & de Garcia, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Kuperman, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Despite theoretical models suggesting that the orthographic form of compound words influence their processing, empirical evidence regarding the impact of spacing remains nuanced.
Several studies indicate that spaced compounds generally incur a processing cost relative to unspaced counterparts.

For instance, Juhasz and Berkowitz (2011) reported longer reading times in eye-tracking for spaced compounds and Elsherif and Catling (2023) observed that spaced words resulted in slower decision times during memory tasks.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Juhasz and Berkowitz (2011)</ref> reported longer reading times in eye-tracking for spaced compounds and <ref type="bibr">Elsherif and Catling (2023)</ref> observed that spaced words resulted in slower decision times during memory tasks.

text.text: Furthermore, research has consistently shown that the AoA of the constituent morphemes influence processing speed when compounds are presented in their spaced form, suggesting that spacing may modulate how lexical components are integrated (Elsherif & Catling, 2021 , 2024; Elsherif et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Furthermore, research has consistently shown that the AoA of the constituent morphemes influence processing speed when compounds are presented in their spaced form, suggesting that spacing may modulate how lexical components are integrated <ref type="bibr">(Elsherif & Catling, 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Elsherif et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, some empirical evidence contradicts the general trend; for instance, Inhoff et al. (2000) observed that introducing spaces into German compounds actually facilitated processing speed, and Elsherif and Catling (2024) found that spaced compounds were recognized more quickly than unspaced compounds in lexical decision tasks.
text.formatted: However, some empirical evidence contradicts the general trend; for instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Inhoff et al. (2000)</ref> observed that introducing spaces into German compounds actually facilitated processing speed, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Elsherif and Catling (2024)</ref> found that spaced compounds were recognized more quickly than unspaced compounds in lexical decision tasks.

text.text: These conflicting findings highlight a significant lack of consensus in the literature, suggesting that the processing costs of spaced versus unspaced compounds may be highly task-dependent.
The likelihood of observing an AoA effect, whether for the compound as a whole or for its individual constituents, is fundamentally linked to orthographic spacing.
Evidence consistently demonstrates that the AoA of the whole compound reliably influences processing across both spaced and unspaced presentations (Elsherif et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Evidence consistently demonstrates that the AoA of the whole compound reliably influences processing across both spaced and unspaced presentations <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Elsherif et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, the role of morphemic AoA is more variable: it appears to drive processing speed primarily when compounds are presented in their spaced form.

Specifically, research has shown that the AoA of the modifier and head constituents contribute to naming latencies and memory task performance only when the word is spaced (Elsherif et al., 2019; Elsherif & Catling, 2023 , 2024).
text.formatted: Specifically, research has shown that the AoA of the modifier and head constituents contribute to naming latencies and memory task performance only when the word is spaced <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Elsherif et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Elsherif & Catling, 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that the presence of a space may shift the cognitive load, forcing the system to rely more heavily on constituent-level semantic representations during lexical processing.

Given the inconsistent evidence for these effects in eye-tracking, the role of constituent AoA in whole-word processing remains a critical, and unresolved, variable, particularly under varying orthographic conditions.
To date, only one eye-tracking study has examined AoA effects in unspaced compound words during reading. Juhasz (2018) investigated the influence of AoA in 48 young adults.
text.formatted: To date, only one eye-tracking study has examined AoA effects in unspaced compound words during reading. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Juhasz (2018)</ref> investigated the influence of AoA in 48 young adults.

text.text: The authors observed significant AoA effects in GD and TFD but not in FFD and SFD.
Juhasz observed that early-acquired compound words were processed more rapidly than later-acquired words, as evidenced by shorter gaze duration and total reading times.
However, there was no effect of individual constituents on reading times.
The authors concluded that the representations of the constituents might not be automatically activated during the processing of the whole compound word.

Similarly, Kuperman and Bertram (2013) found that reaction times are affected by the properties of the compound word, rather than by the properties of its constituents (but see Elsherif et al., 2019; Elsherif & Catling, 2021 , 2024 , 2026; Juhasz et al., 2003).

text.text: In sum, while the AoA effect is consistently observed in compound words themselves, the extent to which their constituents contribute to reading behavior remains contentious.
Taken together, the AoA effect is a robust predictor of word recognition across the lifespan and various tasks.
According to the integrated account, early-acquired words form stronger, more integrated mappings between orthographic, phonological, and semantic representations.
However, the bulk of this evidence stems from monomorphemic words in young adults using response-based tasks.
Crucially, three gaps remain that prevent a complete understanding of how developmental learning shapes the mental lexicon.

First, while the AoA effect is observed in older adults via behavioral measures, its manifestation in the ecologically valid context of reading, specifically via eye-movement metrics, remains unexplored.

Second, although whole-word AoA reliably influences compound processing, the role of constituent-level AoA is contentious, with evidence suggesting that morphemic influences may be masked or constrained by the way a word is visually presented.

Third, this potential modulation by orthographic format (spaced vs. unspaced) suggests that spacing alters the fundamental balance between holistic and decomposed processing, a mechanism that has yet to be tested in naturalistic reading.

To address these limitations, the present study uses eye-tracking during sentence reading to investigate how the AoA effect is modulated by reader age (young vs. older adults) and compound word format, thereby testing the generalizability of the Integrated Account to more complex populations and lexical items.
By examining AoA effects across both spaced and unspaced compounds, this study provides a unique window into how lexical access evolves across the adult lifespan.

While foundational eye-tracking research has established the AoA effect for monomorphemic words (e.g., , Dirix & Duyck, 2017a , 2017b; Guedea et al., 2025; Juhasz et al., 2011; Juhasz & Rayner, 2006; Juhasz & Sheridan, 2020) and compound words (Juhasz, 2018), little is known about how these effects manifest in older adults, whose decades of additional linguistic experience may fundamentally reshape early-learned advantages.
text.formatted: While foundational eye-tracking research has established the AoA effect for monomorphemic words (e.g., , <ref type="bibr">Dirix & Duyck, 2017a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">, 2017b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Guedea et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Juhasz et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Juhasz & Rayner, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Juhasz & Sheridan, 2020)</ref> and compound words <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Juhasz, 2018)</ref>, little is known about how these effects manifest in older adults, whose decades of additional linguistic experience may fundamentally reshape early-learned advantages.

text.text: Thus, this study investigates how AoA influences reading behaviour across unspaced and spaced compound words and across the adult lifespan (young and older adulthood).

Crucially, the orthographic format of compounds, spaced versus unspaced, serves as a functional probe to reveal whether this increased experience facilitates a more holistic approach to lexical access or maintains a reliance on constituent decomposition.

By integrating these factors, this research addresses the current gap in ageing literature and provides a rigorous test of whether the Integrated Account's predictions generalize to complex, multi-morphemic structures in naturalistic reading.
We conducted two experiments to evaluate the role of the AoA effect in compound word processing across the lifespan.
By manipulating orthographic spacing (spaced vs. unspaced), we sought to determine whether the AoA effect is located at the lexical/semantic level across the lifespan, as posited by Juhasz (2018).
text.formatted: By manipulating orthographic spacing (spaced vs. unspaced), we sought to determine whether the AoA effect is located at the lexical/semantic level across the lifespan, as posited by <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Juhasz (2018)</ref>.

text.text: We examined whether introducing a space into typically unspaced compound words increased readers' reliance on the earlyacquired semantic representations of the constituent morphemes.
Experiment 1 therefore aimed to test AoA effects in unspaced compound words presented within sentences in young and older adults.
Experiment 2 investigated these effects when the same words were presented spaced, to assess how spacing influenced the AoA effect in young and older adults.
We asked the following research questions: RQ1: Is the AoA effect present in orthographic spacing across the lifespan?
RQ2: How do orthographic spacing and age interact to influence the AoA effect during compound word processing?

The following predictions in addressing RQ1 was that in line with previous research (e.g., see review by Elsherif et al., 2023; Inhoff et al., 2000), we first expected a main effect of AoA, where earlier acquired words are more processed more quickly than late-acquired words, and a main effect of spacing, where unspaced words are processed more quickly than spaced words.
text.formatted: The following predictions in addressing RQ1 was that in line with previous research (e.g., see review by <ref type="bibr">Elsherif et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Inhoff et al., 2000)</ref>, we first expected a main effect of AoA, where earlier acquired words are more processed more quickly than late-acquired words, and a main effect of spacing, where unspaced words are processed more quickly than spaced words.

text.text: Building upon this, our predictions for RQ2 expected a smaller AoA effect for spaced compound words than unspaced compound words because the separation may impede direct access to the full compound's lexical-semantic representation (Elsherif, Kirkden et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Building upon this, our predictions for RQ2 expected a smaller AoA effect for spaced compound words than unspaced compound words because the separation may impede direct access to the full compound's lexical-semantic representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Elsherif, Kirkden et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This weakening could also increase competition between the constituents, particularly for later-learned words.
We also predicted a two-way interaction between AoA and age.
Specifically, we expected the AoA effect to be smaller for older adults than for younger adults.
Decades of additional linguistic experience may allow the lexicalsemantic networks of later-learned words to become more entrenched, narrowing the processing gap between early and late acquisitions.
Furthermore, the use of eye-tracking allows for the precise measurement of cognitive processes across different stages of reading.
Earlier processing measures (e.g., FFD, SFD and GD) primarily reflect initial word identification time and lexical access.
Later measures such as TFD capture post-lexical processing, such as semantic integration.
The pattern of AoA effects across these measures can therefore be used to further evaluate theoretical accounts.

Effects restricted to earlierstage reading (e.g., FFD, GD) would support the Mapping Theory, which attributes AoA advantages to stronger, early-formed mappings created during periods of high neural plasticity.

Effects limited to the later stage (TFD/total reading time) would primarily support the Representation Theory, which emphasises that early-learned words are more deeply embedded in semantic networks and thus bias lexical retrieval.

Effects observed across both early and late measures would support the integrated account, where early-acquired words benefit simultaneously from richer semantic networks and more efficient orthographic-tophonological mappings.

text.text: PANGEA power calculations indicated that a sample size of 30 participants per experiment (i.e., spaced x unspaced in young adults (Experiments 1 and 2) and spaced x unspaced in older adults (Experiments 3 and 4) reading 209 items would yield statistical power exceeding 1 -ẞ = .80 for the target two-way interaction effects.
To achieve this, we recruited 60 younger adults (30 assigned to unspaced and 30 assigned to spaced conditions) and 30 older adults (who completed both spaced and unspaced conditions).

Whereas previous eye-tracking benchmarks in compound reading relied on smaller item sets (e.g., 120 items in Juhasz, 2018), testing all 209 items led to 90 participants producing a total of 25,080 trials, maximising statistical power by substantially reducing item-level standard errors (Brysbaert, 2018).

A final sample of 90 participants took part in the study.

Thirty young adults (18-24 years) participated in Experiment 1; a second group of 30 young adults (18-23 years) participated in Experiment 2; and 30 older adults (61-85 years) participated in Experiments 3 and 4.

A further three young adults were excluded from Experiment 1 due to experimenter error in recording eye-movement data, and one further young adult was excluded from Experiment 2 for reporting dyslexia.
The young adult participants were first-and second-year undergraduate students from the School of Psychology and Vision Sciences at the University of Leicester.
Older adult participants were recruited from the local community in Leicester.
In accordance with APA guidelines, we reported the self-declared ethnic heritage of the participants, confirming the diversity of the UK sample.

Importantly, all participants were classed as native British English speakers: all participants completed their education within the British education system and reported using British English as their primary language from the age of three years.
The study received ethical approval from the University of Leicester Ethics Committee (ref: 39830).
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.
Young adults received course credit in exchange for participation, while older adults were compensated with a £30 voucher per experiment (£60 total).
All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and identified English as their primary language.

text.text: Thirty young adults read unspaced compound words in sentences (Experiment 1), while another thirty young adults read spaced compound words in sentences (Experiment 2).
Older adults completed two separate eye-tracking sessions: one for the unspaced and one for the spaced compound words.

Due to the practical challenges of recruiting from the older adult population, a within-subjects design was employed for the spacing manipulation to maximize statistical power and account for individual variability.

To control for potential order effects and practice effects associated with the within-subjects design, the order of the spacing manipulation was fully counterbalanced across older adult participants.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: those who completed the unspaced session first and those who completed the spaced session first.
Each older adult session consisted of instructions, task completion and post-task assessments, with Session 1 lasting approximately two hours and Session 2 lasting one hour.
The sessions were split by seven days, to minimise potential carryover, learning, and fatigue effects.
Therefore, the total duration for each older adult participant across the entire study was approximately 3 hours.
Participants were tested individually in a dimmed room.
Eye movements were recorded via an Eyelink 1000 Plus tower-mounted eye-tracker (SR Research, Ltd., Canada).
This system has an angular resolution of less than .01 Root Mean Square.
Right-eye movements were sampled at 1000Hz using corneal reflection and pupil tracking.
A chin and forehead rest were used to reduce head movements, and a VPixx response box was used to collect manual responses.
Sentences were displayed on a 19-inch monitor, at a 60 cm viewing distance, with each letter subtended approximately 1° horizontally.
Sentence stimuli were displayed in 14-point Courier New font as black text on a white background.
Sentences were shown as a single line of text.
Participants were instructed to read each sentence naturally and for comprehension.
At the start of the experiment, a 3-point horizontal calibration was performed along the same line as the sentence presentation, ensuring spatial accuracy of 0.30° or better for all participants.
Calibration accuracy was checked before each trial.
To maintain high spatial precision throughout the session, recalibration was conducted whenever a participant took a break and additionally at the experimenter's discretion.
At the start of each trial, a fixation cross (equal in size to one character space) appeared on the left side of the display.
Once the participant fixated this location, the cross disappeared, and the sentence stimulus was presented, with its first letter replacing the cross.
Participants were instructed to read each sentence naturally and silently, and to then look toward a fixation point located to the right of the sentence.
They were also instructed to press a key on a response box to indicate that they had completed reading.
The sentence then disappeared and was either followed by a comprehension question or the next trial.
Comprehension questions were presented on 24% of trials.
Half the questions required a "yes" response and half a "no" response.
Participants responded by pressing one of two keys on the response box.
For unspaced compound words, response accuracy was 96% and 97% for young and older adults, respectively; for spaced compound words, accuracy was 98% for both groups.
Participants were offered breaks approximately every 15 minutes and could take additional breaks as needed.
Once data collection was complete, we used SR Research DataViewer to process and prepare the eye-tracking data for analysis.
We then pre-processed the data following standard quality-control protocols for reading eye-tracking paradigms (e.g., Inhoff & Radach, 1998; Rayner, 1998).

text.text: First, we removed long fixations exceeding 1200ms, as indicators of tracking artefacts or tracker loss.
Following that step, we combined brief fixations to account for oculomotor drift and small saccadic corrections.

Fixations lasting less than 80ms that occurred within 0.5 of the visual angle of an adjacent fixation were combined, as were fixations under 120 ms occurring within 1.25 degrees apart (see review by Drieghe et al., 2026).

text.text: Any remaining unmerged fixations with durations under 80ms were discarded, as they fall below the perceptual threshold necessary for lexical processing.
Data loss constituted 0.77% of the total data.
We then also removed the compound word 'background', as participants scored more than 80% error on the associated comprehension question; this represented a data loss of 0.48% of the remaining data.

To investigate whether the AoA effect on compound word processing is modulated by age and orthographic spacing, our analysis proceeds in two stages.
First, we provide granular Bayesian sub-analyses for each experimental condition (spaced and unspaced, for both young and older adults).
Second, we integrate the data from all conditions into a global linear mixed-effects model (the primary analysis).
This approach directly tests the three-way interaction between age, spacing, and our core lexical predictors to evaluate the Integrated Account.
This multi-stage approach ensures that our conclusions regarding the high-level interaction are anchored by the established, robust presence of AoA effects at the individual condition level.
We used a hybrid statistical approach to ensure the robustness of our findings.

The Bayesian sub-analyses provide a nuanced estimation of individual effects without the binary constraints of traditional significance testing, allowing for a granular examination of AoA across conditions.
Conversely, our global analysis uses Likelihood Ratio Tests to demonstrate that the three-way interaction provides a significantly better fit to the data than simpler models.
By verifying our results across both statistical philosophies, we establish that our findings are not artifacts of a single methodological framework.
Details of these models are provided below, beginning with our sub-analyses.
We started with four models, to assess the effect of psycholinguistic predictors on the processing of spaced and unspaced compound words in young and older adults separately.
Models 1 and 2 examined unspaced and spaced compound words in young adults respectively.
Models 3 and 4 examined unspaced and spaced compound words in older adults respectively.

In the baseline models, the mean-centred fixed effects were: compound word frequency, frequency of both the modifier and head lexemes, and word length of the compound word (see supplementary materials for baseline models).
The outcome variables were the following standard eye-movement measures on the target compound word (see Rayner, 2009): FFD, SFD, GD and total reading time.
