Following the granular sub-analyses, we integrated data from both age groups and spacing conditions to formally test the Integrated Account of AoA.

As established in our introduction, this account posits that lexical retrieval is a dynamic process where cognitive demands, such as those imposed by non-canonical spacing or age-related changes, are modulated by a word's AoA.

If this framework holds, we should observe that the processing of compound words is not merely the sum of independent factors, but a complex interaction where AoA acts as a buffer against the processing costs associated with spacing and ageing.
To specifically test whether AoA and familiarity and Imageability can be disentangled, we compared models containing both terms, Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC).
Note that for effects where the likelihood ratio test yielded a critical value near the standard statistical significance threshold (X2 = 3.84 to 4.50), BIC values show a slight increase.

This reflects the conservative complexity penalty function of BIC under large sample sizes (N), where a model's log-likelihood fit improvement (X2) must exceed the penalty term ln(N) to achieve a decrease in BIC.
We report both metrics for transparency, relying on likelihood ratio tests for hypothesis testing.

To evaluate this, we conducted a global linear mixed-effects model assessing the three-way interaction of age, spacing, and our core lexical predictors (frequency, familiarity, AoA, and imageability).

This model serves as the primary analysis to answer our core research question: whether older readers can overcome the structural costs of spaced compound words through the established advantages of early-acquired lexical representations.
Fixed effects were sum-coded to allow for a direct assessment of group and condition differences (spacing: -1 = unspaced,1 = spaced; age: -1 = older adults,1 = young adults).

The present study used eye-tracking to investigate how AoA influences compound word processing, focusing specifically on how these effects are modulated by younger and older adults and word spacing.
Our findings revealed that the age at which participants learned a compound word significantly influenced eye movements during reading.
Words acquired earlier in life were generally associated with fewer fixations in young adults, across spaced and unspaced compound words.
This supports previous findings, that the AoA of compound words, whether presented spaced or unspaced, influences eye movements in young adults (Juhasz, 2018).
text.formatted: This supports previous findings, that the AoA of compound words, whether presented spaced or unspaced, influences eye movements in young adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Juhasz, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, in older adults, we only observed an AoA effect during the reading of unspaced compound words.
RQ1: AoA, orthographic spacing across the lifespan Lexical Access in Young Adults: The Impact of AoA and Spacing

When reading unspaced and spaced compound words, we observed in young adults that the AoA of the compound (as well as its familiarity) contributed to processing across eyetracking measures, replicating Juhasz (2018).
text.formatted: When reading unspaced and spaced compound words, we observed in young adults that the AoA of the compound (as well as its familiarity) contributed to processing across eyetracking measures, replicating <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Juhasz (2018)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we observed that there were fewer and smaller fixations on words that were acquired earlier, as well as on words that were more frequent and more familiar.

This indicates that unspaced and spaced compound words are processed more quickly when they are acquired earlier in life, in eye-movement measures that reflect both early first-pass reading and later syntactic integration.

The observation of an AoA effect in both unspaced and spaced compound words further indicates that these words are processed as a single lexical representation, rather than as individual constituents, irrespective of spacing.

An effect of word length was also observed, but only in gaze duration and total fixation duration for unspaced compound words, and in all measures except total fixation duration for spaced compound words.
There was an interaction between AoA and spacing in young adults.

Across first fixation duration, single fixation duration and gaze duration, the slope of the AoA effect was steeper when the compound word was presented as an unspaced item, rather than as a spaced item.
Thus, we observed that the AoA effect was stronger when processing requires direct access to the whole-word lexical representation, rather than via the constituent morphemes.
In spaced compound words, the spacing splits the compound word into its two constituents.

This potentially introduces initial competition between the meaning of the compound word and the meanings of its constituent morphemes, at first diluting the facilitatory effect of acquiring the compound word earlier in life.
However, in total fixation duration, the slope of the AoA effect was steeper when the compound word was presented as a spaced item, rather than as an unspaced item.

Thus, in total fixation duration, which indexes processing time once readers have integrated the constituent morphemes into a single lexical representation, there is no longer any competition-mediated dilution of the AoA effect.
Instead, the AoA effect is strengthened, with readers benefitting from having acquired both the constituents, and the whole compound, earlier in life (Brooks & de Garcia, 2015).
text.formatted: Instead, the AoA effect is strengthened, with readers benefitting from having acquired both the constituents, and the whole compound, earlier in life <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brooks & de Garcia, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This process is also reflected in imageability, which was stronger for spaced compound words than unspaced compound words in total fixation duration, indicating that the AoA has a lexical-semantic component.
When reading unspaced compound words, we observed in older adults that the AoA of the compound (as well as its familiarity) contributed to processing across eye-tracking measures.
Here, we observed that there were fewer and smaller fixations on words that were acquired earlier, as well as on words that were more frequent and more familiar.

This indicates that unspaced compound words are processed more quickly when they are acquired earlier in life, in eye-movement measures that reflect both early first-pass reading and later syntactic integration.
The observation of an AoA effect in unspaced compound words indicates that these words were being processed as a single lexical representation, rather than as individual constituents.

The findings also support the suggestion that the AoA effect can be observed from the point of early first-pass measures, which index low-level processing between orthography and phonology, in line with Elsherif and Catling's (2021, 2023) argument.
text.formatted: The findings also support the suggestion that the AoA effect can be observed from the point of early first-pass measures, which index low-level processing between orthography and phonology, in line with <ref type="bibr">Elsherif and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Catling's (2021, 2023)</ref> argument.

text.text: Critically, these results underscore the role of linguistic entrenchment in the mature lexicon.
Despite decades of additional language experience, older adults demonstrate that the lexical-semantic networks formed early in life remain highly stable and efficient (e.g., Davies et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Despite decades of additional language experience, older adults demonstrate that the lexical-semantic networks formed early in life remain highly stable and efficient (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Davies et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This entrenchment allows older readers to maintain a unified processing strategy for unspaced compounds, effectively leveraging their long-standing linguistic knowledge to facilitate rapid whole-word retrieval.

By maintaining this consistent AoA advantage, older adults demonstrate that their mental lexicon does not merely expand or degrade with age, but rather becomes more refined, allowing for the stable, efficient processing of familiar, early-acquired word forms when they are presented in their standard orthographic configuration.

An effect of word length was also observed in unspaced compound words, but only in gaze duration and total fixation duration, indicating lengthbased processing remains a secondary, later-stage constraint compared to the primary influence of AoA and familiarity.
In older adults, the processing of spaced compound words was unaffected by AoA across all eye-tracking measures.
We observed effects of only word length and semantic transparency in gaze duration and total fixation duration.
Thus, shorter compound words received shorter fixations than longer compound words and semantically transparent compound words received fewer fixations than semantically opaque compound words.
An effect of familiarity was only observed in total fixation duration.
In older adults, the absence of an AoA effect in spaced compound words likely stems from the dual nature of linguistic entrenchment in the mature lexicon (Ramscar et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In older adults, the absence of an AoA effect in spaced compound words likely stems from the dual nature of linguistic entrenchment in the mature lexicon <ref type="bibr">(Ramscar et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Through decades of cumulative language exposure, older adults develop highly entrenched, rigid orthographic-semantic representations for unspaced compounds.

Consequently, encountering an artificially spaced compound (e.g., sweet corn) severely violates these entrenched orthographic expectations, causing an immediate parsing failure that is further exacerbated by age-related reductions in perceptual span (Rayner et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Consequently, encountering an artificially spaced compound (e.g., sweet corn) severely violates these entrenched orthographic expectations, causing an immediate parsing failure that is further exacerbated by age-related reductions in perceptual span <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Rayner et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zhang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Because this unexpected space is included, it impedes direct lexical access and forces older adults to rely on lower-level, early word-level attributes like length (Inhoff et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Because this unexpected space is included, it impedes direct lexical access and forces older adults to rely on lower-level, early word-level attributes like length <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Inhoff et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: This effectively allows AoA to be bypassed by immediate low-level processing.
Furthermore, because artificially spaced compounds are initially misparsed as orthographically illegal non-compounds, the reading process becomes bottlenecked at the low-level orthographic stages.

During this stage, lexical-semantic variables (e.g. ,AoA) are prevented from producing their influence on gaze duration and total fixation durations, thereby constraining the extent to which relational semantic properties (e.g., semantic transparency) can facilitate reading times.
Crucially these constraints persist despite semantic processing typically playing a larger role in longer words (Cortese & Schock, 2013).
text.formatted: Crucially these constraints persist despite semantic processing typically playing a larger role in longer words <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Cortese & Schock, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, this orthographic expectation manifests primarily in early eye-movement metrics: age-related divergence between young and older adults was shown in FFD and SFD, capturing the initial perceptual parsing and constituent processing of first lexeme.
In contrast, in TFD, which indexes late stage semantic integration and re-reading, AoA and spacing became highly similar between young and older adults.

This indicates while orthographic familiarity, entrenched expectations, and reduced visual span disrupts early constituent recognition for older adults temporarily, while late-stage lexical integration and semantic consolidation operate similarly across age groups once the full compound structure is evaluated.

We can therefore conclude that the processing of compound words relies on a shifting balance between orthographic cues and long-term lexical knowledge, which evolves significantly across the lifespan.
Furthermore, we investigated the interactions between spacing and AoA.
We found that unspaced compound words showed the largest effects of AoA.
In total fixation duration, the AoA effect was stronger in spaced than unspaced compound words.

The divergence between early and late measures suggests that while AoA initially facilitates the holistic recognition of unspaced compounds, its role shifts during the later stages of processing for spaced compounds.
The presence of a space forces the reader to work harder to assemble the meaning of the two parts.

This creates a larger processing gap: early-acquired words remain easy to synthesize because the brain has strong, pre-existing 'shortcuts' for them, whereas later-acquired words require significantly more effort to combine, leading to longer fixation durations.

This aligns with the representation theory proposed by Brysbaert et al. (2000), which posits that the semantic nodes for early-acquired words are more centrally located and more densely connected with the mental lexicon.
text.formatted: This aligns with the representation theory proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Brysbaert et al. (2000)</ref>, which posits that the semantic nodes for early-acquired words are more centrally located and more densely connected with the mental lexicon.

text.text: Consequently, these findings suggest that the AoA is a structural characteristic of how linguistic information is organised and retrieved across the lifespan.

This process is also reflected in imageability, familiarity, and frequency which was stronger for spaced compound words than unspaced compound words in total fixation duration, indicating that the AoA has a lexical-semantic component.
We also observed a two-way interaction between ageing and AoA.
The influence of AoA was less pronounced in older adults compared to younger adults, as observed across all duration measures.
The reduced AoA effect in older readers may reflect a shift in how the mental lexicon organises itself over time.

Specifically, as the semantic network becomes more dense with age, the foundational nodes established by early-acquired words provide a more efficient framework for processing complex compounds, leading to a decline in the AoA effect.
This process is also reflected in imageability, familiarity, and frequency which showed an age-related decline such that these measures decrease with age.

Additionally, the finding that the AoA effect is partially aligned with the suggestion the AoA effect is a result of time: early-acquired words are processed more quickly only because, having been learned first, they are encountered significantly more often over the course of the lifespan than words acquired later (i.e., the cumulative frequency explanation; Lewis, 1999).
text.formatted: Additionally, the finding that the AoA effect is partially aligned with the suggestion the AoA effect is a result of time: early-acquired words are processed more quickly only because, having been learned first, they are encountered significantly more often over the course of the lifespan than words acquired later (i.e., the cumulative frequency explanation; <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Lewis, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, in line with Monaghan and Ellis (2010), the finding that the AoA effect lessens with age may reflect a shift in network efficiency: as the semantic system matures and becomes more interconnected, the structural headstart provided by early-acquired nodes may become less vital for fluent compound word processing.
text.formatted: On the other hand, in line with <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Monaghan and Ellis (2010)</ref>, the finding that the AoA effect lessens with age may reflect a shift in network efficiency: as the semantic system matures and becomes more interconnected, the structural headstart provided by early-acquired nodes may become less vital for fluent compound word processing.

text.text: The interaction of spacing and AoA, as well as the interaction between AoA and ageing can be both explained by the integrated account.
According to this framework, the In contrast, the age-related decline of the AoA effect reflects the developmental changes within the semantic hub itself.
Over decades of cumulative reading experience, later-acquired words received repeated exposures and continued semantic integration (see Bybee, 2011 for further explanation).
This lifelong exposure solidifies late-learned representations within the semantic network, effectively narrowing the structural processing gap between early-and late-acquired compound words.
In older adults, the semantic hub becomes highly dense and interconnected.
Consequently, the advantage of early-acquired words over late-acquired words becomes less critical for fluent holistic word recognition.

Our results reveal that the AoA effect depends on the direct mapping and maturational state of the semantic network, which is in line with linguistic entrenchment for older adults (Davies et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Our results reveal that the AoA effect depends on the direct mapping and maturational state of the semantic network, which is in line with linguistic entrenchment for older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Davies et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: While our primary focus rests on the two-way interactions (Spacing * AoA, Age * AoA), evaluating the full interaction pattern helps illustrate the operational limits of lexical processing across conditions.
Unspaced compounds maintain a consistent, albeit smaller, AoA advantage across the adult lifespan.

In contrast, spaced compounds exhibit a floor effect in older adults, where the structural disruption of the space combined with age-related orthographic rigidity eliminates the whole-word AoA advantage.

In line with the Integrated Account (Brysbaert & Ellis, 2016; Chang et al., 2019; Elsherif et al., 2023), these pattern differences demonstrate that whole-word AoA influences processing primarily when readers can access holistic representations, whereas visual disruption forces older readers to shift toward constituent-level parsing (for full three-way model parameters and extended theoretical breakdown, see Supplementary Material Table S17).

text.text: The findings from this study could also inform the development of quantitative models of eye movement control, particularly those designed for monolingual, native language reading.
Examples of existing models include E-Z Reader (e.g., Rayner et al., 2006; Reichle, 2021; Reichle et al., 2012) and SWIFT (e.g., Engbert et al., 2005; Laubrock et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Examples of existing models include E-Z Reader (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Rayner et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Reichle, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Reichle et al., 2012)</ref> and SWIFT (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Engbert et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Laubrock et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, E-Z Reader has successfully simulated how eye movements in reading differ with age (Rayner et al., 2006; Laubrock et al., 2006 showed similar results with SWIFT).
text.formatted: For instance, E-Z Reader has successfully simulated how eye movements in reading differ with age <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Rayner et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Laubrock et al., 2006</ref> showed similar results with SWIFT).

text.text: While E-Z Reader primarily focuses on the word frequency effect, it can, in theory, explain AoArelated reading development in children by considering cumulative frequency.
More specifically, E-Z Reader suggests that the initial stages of accessing a word are influenced by its properties, including how often it occurs.
Words learned later in life are generally encountered less often and have lower subjective frequencies than words learned earlier.
However, it is important to clarify that this is not a universal rule for all words acquired throughout life.
Some words learned later might be encountered more frequently and have higher subjective frequencies but still be processed more slowly than earlier-acquired words.
Crucially, the current version of the E-Z Reader model addresses AoA only indirectly.

While cumulative frequency and a word's frequency trajectory during development do correlate with AoA, the model lacks explicit mechanisms to capture the subtle, potentially qualitative differences in how words are represented and processed due to AoA itself (Zevin & Seidenberg, 2002 , 2004).
text.formatted: While cumulative frequency and a word's frequency trajectory during development do correlate with AoA, the model lacks explicit mechanisms to capture the subtle, potentially qualitative differences in how words are represented and processed due to AoA itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">(Zevin & Seidenberg, 2002</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: For example, AoA effects often remain even when frequency is accounted for, indicating that the timing of learning uniquely impacts how words are stored and accessed.

Therefore, future adaptations of models such as E-Z Reader, especially when considering the entire lifespan, would benefit from including direct parameters that account for AoA's independent contributions to how we process words and control our eye movements during reading.
Although our preliminary analyses incorporated phonological controls to manage noise in reading data, we have chosen to use more parsimonious models for this report.
This approach was adopted to secure more stable regression estimates and mitigate the risks associated with overparameterisation (Achen, 2005).
text.formatted: This approach was adopted to secure more stable regression estimates and mitigate the risks associated with overparameterisation <ref type="bibr">(Achen, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: By transitioning to more parsimonious models, we secured more reliable estimates and mitigated the risk of Type I errors associated with high-dimensional model structures.
Crucially, our subsequent Bayesian analysis demonstrated that the core AoA effects remained robust regardless of this simplification.
This process therefore served as a rigorous validation step, significantly increasing our confidence in the consistency and stability of these findings.
A further limitation of our stimuli relates to the representation of spaced compound words.
While we included unspaced compounds, our set did not feature compounds that are conventionally spaced in natural language (e.g., 'fast food').

Consequently, our findings may not fully capture the processing nuances involved in reading natural, open-compound forms, which differ structurally from both closed-form compounds and simple non-compound words.

Future research should prioritise the inclusion of these naturally spaced compounds to determine if the morphological decomposition processes we observed remain consistent when the orthographic boundary is explicitly marked by a space, rather than implied through constituent combination to enhance the study's ecological validity.
We must also note a limitation in our experimental design regarding participant allocation.

While our younger adult cohort consisted of two distinct groups, 30 participants for the unspaced condition and a separate 30 for the spaced condition, our older adult sample comprised 30 individuals who completed both conditions.

To mitigate potential confounding variables such as practice effects or cumulative fatigue inherent in within-subjects designs, we implemented a mandatory one-week interval between testing sessions to minimise carryover effects and the order of the spaced and unspaced conditions was systematically counterbalanced across participants for older adults.

While these measures were designed to isolate the effects of the experimental conditions, future research should aim for a fully independent design across all cohorts to further ensure that performance is not inadvertently influenced by variations in exposure or testing order.
In conclusion, our research provides robust evidence for the influence of AoA on compound word processing, though the manifestation of this effect is modulated by both format and cognitive task.
Our eye-tracking data suggests that while AoA influences all levels of lexical retrieval in young adults, this effect is attenuated in older adults, likely due to increased semantic entrenchment.
Our findings also reveal a critical boundary: the effect is modulated by compound format in older adults.
This suggests that the mental lexicon undergoes a qualitative shift with age.

The space in compound words forces a transition toward constituent-level processing; because spaced constituents are orthographically distinct, they likely compete for lexical selection rather than converging into a unified representation.
Consequently, the structural integration typically afforded to early-acquired words is disrupted.
We propose that because the ageing lexicon is more densely interconnected, older adults rely on a highly entrenched, unified semantic structure.

When a compound word is presented with a space, this structure is challenged; the reader must resolve the competition between the individual lexemes and the compound entry itself, a process that negates the processing advantage of early acquisition.

This refinement to the Integrated Account highlights that while AoA remains a fundamental driver of lexical retrieval, its manifestation is sensitive to the interplay between linguistic format and the adaptive plasticity of the ageing brain.

While existing eye-tracking models can partially account for our findings, it remains an open question as to whether quantitative models of eye-movement control, developed primarily to explain word frequency (such as E-Z Reader and SWIFT), can formally simulate the observed AoA effect across the lifespan in more complex words.
Addressing this gap will be crucial for developing a truly unified theory of reading that accounts for how lexical plasticity and orthographic complexity interact as we age.
We deviated from our pre-registration by examining two-way interactions (AoA * aging and AoA * spacing) rather than three-way interactions (AoA * aging * spacing).
This adjustment was made because our sample lacked sufficient statistical power to test three-way interactions.
To adhere to principles of Open Scholarship, analysis and figures for the three-way interactions are provided in the Supplementary Materials.

In summary, while both whole-compound AoA and familiarity explain significant variance beyond imageability when evaluated independently for both word types, their incremental effects exhibit contrasting time-courses across visual formats.

For unspaced compounds, whole-compound AoA exerts a distinct influence beyond familiarity specifically during firstpass visual inspection (FFD and GD), remaining redundant during single-glance access (SFD) and total processing (TFD).

In contrast, for spaced compounds, whole-compound AoA provides unique predictive value beyond familiarity during initial single-glance access (SFD) and overall reading time (TFD), but is completely subsumed by familiarity during multifixation first-pass inspection (FFD and GD).

text.text: AoA advantage arises from entrenched orthographic-to-phonological mappings formed during early developmental periods of heightened neuroplasticity (Mapping Theory) and the central positioning of early acquired words within the densely connected semantic hub (Representation Account).
The decline of the AoA effect from spaced to unspaced compound words, alongside its age-related decline, indicates that these interactions reflect different mechanisms within the integrated account.
Introducing a space into conventional compound words disrupts the immediate, direct mapping between orthographic representation and the whole-word compound word semantic entry.
This visual separation forces the cognitive system into constituent-level decomposition, triggering competition between the constituent lexemes and the full compound entry.
During early first-pass reading (FFD, SFD, GD), this constituent competition dilutes the immediate processing advantage conferred by early whole-word acquisition.
Visual disruption, therefore, temporarily masks the mapping component during initial lexical access, shifting early processing reliance onto constituent-level properties.
